standard.title: Shipbuilding — Diesel Propulsion System Responsibility — Requirements
standard.sector: Transport Engineering / Marine Engineering and Safety Aids

sectional_committee.name: Marine Engineering and Safety Aids Sectional Committee

standard.description: This standard specifies requirements for system responsibility of marine propulsion plants comprising a diesel engine, gear box, stern gear (spelled 'stem gear' in OCR text), and its control system to ensure cohesive matching and performance of all components in diesel engine driven propulsion plants.
standard.scope: This standard specifies requirements for system responsibility of marine propulsion plants comprising a diesel engine, gear box, stern gear (spelled 'stem gear' in OCR text), and its control system to ensure cohesive matching and performance of all components in diesel engine driven propulsion plants.

version.current_version: First Edition, April 2002 (Reviewed and Reaffirmed in 2023)
supersedes: None (developed as a new dedicated national standard to regulate engineering interface boundaries in marine propulsion plants)

amendments.summary: No active amendments have been issued on this standard (NIL on this copy).

certification.description: Voluntary Quality and System Performance Standard. Unlike safety-critical builders hardware or transport tyres under mandatory statutory Quality Control Orders (QCOs), propulsion system responsibility protocols under IS 15052 are certified on a voluntary basis. However, compliance with this standard is universally mandated inside Indian Navy, Coast Guard, port authorities, and commercial maritime shipbuilding and machinery procurement contracts to ensure unified technical responsibility, prevent component mismatch, and guarantee contract speed.
requirements: When assumed, propulsion system responsibility warrants that the delivered horse power (DHP) sought by the ship designer is successfully delivered to the propeller. If the requisite DHP is not achieved (as noted from torsion meters) or the propeller fails to produce the contractual thrust/speed, the issue must be mutually discussed between the engine manufacturer, gear box builder, stern gear designer, and shipbuilder.

Specifies that the main engine must be capable of delivering its continuous net brake power continuously between the normal maintenance intervals stated by the manufacturer under stated test bed conditions, adjusted to standard reference conditions per IS 3979, and tested per IS 10000 (Part 4).

Allows the engine to deliver overload power immediately after working at continuous power under standard reference conditions. Overload power is strictly limited to 110 percent of the continuous power at a speed corresponding to engine application, for a maximum period of 1 hour without interruptions within a period of 12 hours of operation.
Determines the maximum power an engine can deliver during a specified period and ambient condition, with the fuel stop adjusted and locked so that this limit cannot be exceeded.

Specifies intermittent ratings (increased engine speed for specified durations) and sprint ratings (very short durations at slightly higher speed) for specialized high-speed or tactical marine applications.
Defines service power as the actual power determined under the real-world ambient and operating conditions of a specific engine installation.

The stern gear system must comprise the propeller shaft, intermediate shaft, coupling bolts, bushes, seals, propeller cap, and the propeller itself (fully detailing diameter, pitch, blade area, and moment of inertia).

Enforces a mandatory, comprehensive interface data sheet exchange across the five key stakeholders (Main Engine, Gear Box, Stern Gear, Remote Control, and Shipbuilder) specifying three-view drawings, CG and weights, torsional/axial/lateral vibration calculations, thermal expansion limits, and shaft alignment calculations.
